title: Why memory matters
summary: Every digital system stores data — in flip-flops, register files, SRAM, DRAM or flash. This topic shows where bits live, why systems use a **hierarchy** of memories, and why **locality** makes it work. You will also see how the same SystemVerilog array becomes flip-flops or a real memory.
objectives: Compare flip-flops, register files, SRAM, DRAM and flash as storage.
Describe the memory hierarchy and the processor–memory gap.
Compute the average memory access time and explain locality.
Explain what synthesis builds from an array with asynchronous or synchronous read.

blocks.md: Every digital system stores bits — in very different ways. A **flip-flop** keeps one bit with about 20 transistors and can be read and written by every clock. A **memory array** packs bits far more densely, but gives access to only one or a few words at a time, through an **address**.

blocks.caption: Where bits live

blocks.md: The next subsections show how these storage types are organised in a system. At the end of the topic, *In SystemVerilog* shows how one and the same array in RTL becomes either flip-flops or a real memory.
No single memory is fast, large **and** cheap. Systems therefore stack several levels: small and fast near the processor, large and slow further away.

steps.title: Registers
steps.md: A few hundred to a few thousand bits inside the processor. Read in the same clock cycle.

steps.title: L1 cache
steps.md: Tens of kilobytes of SRAM, about one nanosecond away.

steps.title: L2 / L3 cache
steps.md: Megabytes of SRAM, shared by cores; several to tens of nanoseconds.

steps.title: Main memory
steps.md: Gigabytes of DRAM outside the processor chip; 50–100 ns.

steps.title: Storage
steps.md: Terabytes of flash; tens of microseconds — and it keeps data without power.

blocks.title: Every level is a memory from this course
blocks.md: Registers and caches are **SRAM** or flip-flops, main memory is **DRAM**, storage is **flash**. The following trainings look at each of them in depth.

Processor clocks went up much faster than DRAM speed. A processor at 4 GHz has a cycle time of 0.25 ns; a DRAM access of 80 ns therefore costs about **320 cycles** — time in which the core could have executed hundreds of instructions. This is the **memory wall**.

blocks.caption: Typical latencies seen by a processor

blocks.title: Why it matters to a hardware designer
blocks.md: Most of a chip's area is memory, and most of its waiting is for memory. Choosing the right memory, organisation and interface is often more important than optimising the logic.

steps.title: A typical loop
steps.md: The loop reads an array element by element and updates *sum* every iteration.

steps.title: Spatial locality
steps.md: Addresses close to a recent one are used soon. Caches therefore fetch a whole **line** (here 4 words): one miss, then three hits.

steps.title: Temporal locality
steps.md: A recently used item is used again soon. *sum* stays in the fastest level.

blocks.md:
Locality is what makes a hierarchy work. Its benefit is measured by the **average memory access time**:

> AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty

Example: L1 hit time 1 ns, miss rate 5 %, miss penalty 80 ns → AMAT = 1 + 0.05 × 80 = **5 ns** — much closer to the SRAM than to the DRAM.

blocks.md: In RTL both look like an array. What the hardware becomes depends on **how the array is read**:

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.md: Small and read **asynchronously** → flip-flops or LUT RAM. Large and read **synchronously** → a real memory (SRAM macro or block RAM). A 1024 × 32 array built from flip-flops would need 32 768 flip-flops and a huge multiplexer.

questions.text: A 1024 × 32 array is read with `assign rd = mem[ra];`. What does an ASIC synthesis tool most likely build?
options: Flip-flops and a large read multiplexer

questions.text: Which RTL pattern can be mapped to an SRAM macro or FPGA block RAM?
options: A memory array read inside `always_ff` (synchronous read)
